title: Husic to chair AI inquiry amid productivity crisis
full_text:
Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers has commissioned an inquiry investigating the use of technology to boost Australian productivity amid fears AI may fail to move the dial for a key economic indicator which has sunk to 60-year lows.
Outspoken Labor backbencher Ed Husic will chair a House of Representatives economics committee with its formation announced just days after Dr Chalmers was handed Treasury advice dampening expectations AI will significantly transform Australian inefficiency.
While the Treasurer labelled AI as the biggest economic transformation in his lifetime, analysis from Treasury concluded lacklustre productivity levels may remain intact even after incorporating gains from the technology shift.
Mr Husic said productivity growth across many advanced economies had “stubbornly remained below expectations” despite extraordinary advances in digital technology, artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing and communications.
“While we proudly point to our own tech trailblazers or the ‘first-mover’ eagerness of Australians to adopt and use new technology, that hasn’t always translated into stronger productivity,” Mr Husic said.
“We want this inquiry to move beyond the “tech can improve productivity” mantra, to explore the specifics of how we can do that best.”
While the federal budget assumes average productivity growth of 1.2 per cent a year, the Reserve Bank has warned productivity growth had instead gone backwards, forecasting a contraction of 0.5 per cent for the rest of the year.
Anthropic said Thursday that software it was testing got onto the internet and hacked unsuspecting companies without the AI-maker’s knowledge in three separate incidents dating back to April. The artificial-intelligence vendor didn’t say which companies had been hit, but all three were notified of the incident on Monday, Anthropic said. The news comes one week after OpenAI revealed that its AI technology had broken out of a testing sandbox -- a digital prison that was supposed to be disconnected from the internet -- and hacked the AI company Hugging Face.
A “plausible downside” forecast by Treasury said productivity may remain rooted in its current 0.5 per cent to 0.8 per cent range with AI stalling and only making a “measured contribution” amid constraints on automation across health, education and tourism.
The inquiry would present its report by September 2027 and consider priority technologies, barriers to innovation and international trends to boost productivity.
“We also need to think carefully about Australia’s sovereign capability. The nations that develop, commercialise and deploy critical technologies will be the nations that capture the greatest residual economic and productive value from them,” Mr Husic said.
Treasury analysis shows the transition to a materially higher long-term productivity growth rate of 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent was unlikely to take place within five years.
The analysis may hamper Dr Chalmers’ stated ambition of reviving Australia’s anaemic productivity growth and adds pressure from business leaders for the Albanese government to execute a more ambitious economic reform agenda.
Dr Chalmers, who will use the advice to inform his second Intergenerational Report due in September, said he remained a believer AI was a game changing technology which will impact every part of society.
Economists have said Treasury’s 1.2 per cent productivity growth assumption was “unrealistically high” and the RBA was being optimistic in assuming productivity growth would hit 0.7 per cent by December 2027.
Productivity in the December quarter has been revised to minus 0.5 per cent, down from the previous forecast of 0.2 per cent, according to RBA figures.
Anthony Albanese and Dr Chalmers put fixing productivity on the agenda immediately after the last election win with an August roundtable attended by representatives of industry, unions and civil society. While the government has triggered an overhaul of red and green tape, some business leaders want more aggressive efforts to curb regulations across the economy.
Jobs growth has surged fastest under the Albanese government in many of the least productive sectors of the economy that receive significant government subsidies, such as renewable energy and healthcare.
The Productivity Commission has estimated AI could increase decade-long productivity estimates by at least around 2.3 per cent over 10 years.
Treasury also modelled an upside scenario of 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent productivity growth hinging on AI accelerating the production of ideas themselves along with the proportion of tasks that can be automated.
